value: Virtue yields distinction and wealth alike; what gain for a living being exceeds virtue?
grade_reason: Distinction and wealth from virtue, with nothing greater as gain for living beings, matches Pope's couplet and the structure in all commentaries.

value: There is no gain beyond virtue and no ruin beyond forgetting it.
grade_reason: Matches Parimelazhagar and Pope: no gain above virtue and no ruin above forgetting it.

value: In whatever way you are able, without ceasing, do virtuous deeds wherever they can be done.
grade_reason: Ability-limited, unceasing virtuous action wherever possible matches Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar and Dikshitar.

value: Being stainless in mind is the whole of virtue; everything else is mere noise and show.
grade_reason: Stainless mind as the whole of virtue, the rest being noisy show, matches Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar and Pope.

value: Virtue is what is carried out avoiding four things: envy, craving, anger and harsh words.
grade_reason: Virtue as conduct avoiding envy, craving, anger and harsh speech matches Parimelazhagar and Pope's gloss.

value: Do not say you will attend to it later; do virtue now, for it is the undying companion when you die.
grade_reason: No postponing and an undying companion at death match Pope, Dikshitar and Parimelazhagar.

value: No need to ask what virtue's way is: compare the palanquin's bearer and its rider. The likely traditional sense is that the rider shows virtue's fruit, but the verse could also warn against that inference.
grade_reason: The verse and the traditional sense (fruit of virtue seen between rider and bearer) are named, but the reading only calls this likely and leaves open an opposite sense that no checked source supports, so it does not commit to what the comparison shows.

value: If one does good without letting a day pass idle, that good is a stone blocking the road of one's further births.
grade_reason: A good deed every day as a stone blocking the way of further births matches Pope's gloss, Dikshitar, Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar.

value: Only what comes from virtue is true joy; everything else lies outside it and brings no praise.
grade_reason: Joy only from virtue, with the rest outside and without praise, matches Pope's couplet ('All else extern') and the verse's structure.

value: What one ought to do is virtue; what one ought to escape is blame.
grade_reason: What ought to be done is virtue and what ought to be escaped is blame, matching Manakkudavar closely and Parimelazhagar structurally.

value: A fate of gain brings tireless effort; a fate of loss brings sloth.
grade_reason: Fate of gain brings unflagging effort and fate of loss brings sloth, matching Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar and Pope.

value: A fate of loss makes a person foolish; a fate of gain, when it comes, broadens understanding.
grade_reason: Fate of loss brings folly and fate of gain widens understanding, matching Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar and Pope's gloss.

value: Though one studies many subtle books, one's own innate understanding prevails over them.
grade_reason: One's own innate understanding prevailing over much study matches Manakkudavar and Kalaignar.

value: The world has two distinct natures: wealth is one thing, and being wise is another.
grade_reason: Two natures in the world, wealth and wisdom being separate, matches Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar and Kalaignar.

value: In acquiring wealth, under fate, all that is good can turn out bad and all that is bad can turn out good.
grade_reason: For acquiring wealth, good turning bad and bad turning good under fate matches Parimelazhagar and Pope's gloss.

value: What is not yours will not stay however you guard it; what is yours will not leave though you cast it away.
grade_reason: What is not one's own will not stay and what is one's own will not leave, matching Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar, Pope and Kalaignar.

value: Except as the one who apportions has apportioned, even those who amass crores cannot enjoy it.
grade_reason: Enjoyment only as the apportioner apportioned, even for those amassing crores, matches Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar, Pope and Dikshitar.

value: The destitute would renounce, if only what they are destined to suffer would pass without being inflicted on them.
grade_reason: The destitute would renounce if destined sufferings passed without being inflicted, matching Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar and Dikshitar.

value: Those who see things as good when good comes: why do they grieve when it does not?
grade_reason: Seeing good as good when it comes yet grieving when it does not matches Manakkudavar, Parimelazhagar, Pope and Kalaignar.

value: What is stronger than fate? Even if one devises another way, it arrives first.
grade_reason: Nothing stronger than fate, which gets ahead even of a counter-plan, matches Parimelazhagar, Pope's gloss and Manakkudavar (numbered 374 there).

value: What are called numbers and what are called letters: these two are the eyes of living people.
grade_reason: Numbers and letters as the two eyes of the living matches Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar, Pope and Dikshitar.

value: Only the learned are said to have eyes; the unlearned have two sores on their faces.
grade_reason: Only the learned have eyes and the unlearned have two sores on the face, matching Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar and Pope.

value: Meeting with delight and parting so as to be thought of afterward: such is the scholar's way.
grade_reason: Meeting with delight and parting so as to be remembered as the scholar's work matches Parimelazhagar, Pope's gloss and Manakkudavar.

value: The learned yearn humbly, as the poor do before the rich; those who do not learn are the truly low.
grade_reason: Humble yearning like the poor before the rich, with non-learners as low, closely matches Dikshitar; the exaltation of learners that Parimelazhagar states is only implied.

value: A sand well yields water as far as it is dug; a person's knowledge flows as far as they have learned.
grade_reason: The sand well yields water as far as dug, and knowledge flows as far as learned, matching all sources.

value: Since every land and town becomes one's own through learning, why does anyone stay unlearned until death?
grade_reason: Every land and town becomes one's own for the learned, so why stay unlearned until death, matching Parimelazhagar, Pope's gloss and Dikshitar.

value: Learning gained in a single birth protects a person through seven births.
grade_reason: Learning from one birth protecting through seven births matches Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar, Pope's gloss and Dikshitar.

value: Seeing the world delight in what delights them, the learned long for it all the more.
grade_reason: The learned long for more because the world delights in what delights them, matching Parimelazhagar, Pope's gloss, Dikshitar and Kalaignar.

value: Learning is imperishable, excellent wealth; nothing else is truly wealth.
grade_reason: Learning as imperishable excellent wealth and nothing else as true wealth matches all sources.

value: A person's radiance is abundance of spirit or resolve; disgrace is saying one will live without it.
grade_reason: Radiance as abundance of spirit and disgrace as resolving to live without it matches Parimelazhagar and Pope, and the first half Kalaignar.

value: Like the chastity of faithful women, greatness exists only when one holds oneself to it.
grade_reason: Greatness existing only by self-guarding, like the chastity of single-minded women, matches Parimelazhagar and Pope's gloss.

value: The truly great accomplish, by proper means, deeds that are hard to do.
grade_reason: The great accomplish hard deeds by proper means, matching Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar and Pope.

value: The small-minded do not hold the aim of honouring and following the great.
grade_reason: The small lack the aim of honouring and following the great, matching Parimelazhagar and Pope.

value: When distinction falls to the unworthy, it issues in acts of excess.
grade_reason: Distinction falling on the unworthy issuing in excess matches Parimelazhagar, Pope and Kalaignar.

value: Greatness always bows humbly; smallness adorns itself in self-admiration.
grade_reason: Greatness bows always and smallness adorns itself in self-admiration, matching Manakkudavar, Parimelazhagar and Pope's gloss.

value: Greatness is freedom from arrogance; smallness is riding high on arrogance.
grade_reason: Greatness as absence of arrogance and smallness as riding on it matches Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar, Pope and Kalaignar.

value: Greatness conceals others' failings; smallness speaks of nothing but faults.
grade_reason: Greatness hides others' failings and smallness tells only faults, matching all sources.

value: The lover speaks: she glanced, then looked down, and that was water poured on the love planted between us.
grade_reason: She looked, lowered her head, and that watered the love between them, matching Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar and Pope.

value: The lover speaks: when I look, she looks at the ground; when I do not, she looks at me and smiles softly.
grade_reason: He looks and she looks at the ground; he does not and she looks and smiles softly, matching Pope and Dikshitar.

value: The lover speaks: she does not look at me directly, but smiles as if narrowing one eye.
grade_reason: No direct look but a smile as if narrowing one eye matches Parimelazhagar, Kalaignar and Pope's gloss.

value: Though they speak like strangers, the words of those who are not hostile are quickly understood.
grade_reason: Words of the non-hostile, though spoken as by strangers, being quickly understood matches Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar and Pope's gloss.

value: Small words without anger and looks like an enemy's are the signs of those who pretend to be strangers but are intimate.
grade_reason: Words without anger and enemy-like looks as signs of the intimate who pose as strangers matches Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar and Pope's gloss.

value: When I look, she softens and gently smiles; there is a particular beauty in this graceful one.
grade_reason: She softens and gently smiles when he looks, and has a certain beauty, matches Manakkudavar closely and Kalaignar and Pope's couplet.

value: Glancing in a general way, as strangers do, is found among lovers themselves.
grade_reason: A common glance as of strangers occurring among lovers themselves matches Parimelazhagar, Manakkudavar, Pope's gloss and Dikshitar.

value: When eye meets eye in agreement, the words of the mouth serve no purpose.
grade_reason: When eyes agree, the mouth's words serve no purpose, matching all sources.

position: Nothing is stronger than fate; it arrives ahead of any plan to avoid it.
Parimelazhagar: everything can become fate's route, so fate is the stronger.
Even if fate denies the goal, effort pays the wage of bodily labour.
Those who persist without flagging will put even fate behind them.
If you welcome good fortune, why grieve at the reverse?
Old deeds find their doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows.
Not even saints can remove what is bound to come.
Life moves as a raft moves on a great river.
Life follows its order, as the wise have seen.
The epic names as one of its purposes that past deeds return to exact their fruit.
Kovalan's death is told as his former deed taking effect.

note: The same book says nothing beats fate and that persistence puts fate behind you. Possible readings: 380 describes fate's reach while 620 praises effort, or the two address different audiences. Which one the book favours is unresolved here.
Chapter 38 presents ஊழ் as a force and doesn't explain its source in the verses marked here. Naladiyar 101 makes the moral cause explicit: fate is your own earlier deed returning.
Both use உறற்பால, what is bound to be suffered, which may be a shared idiom. Influence is not established.
Both move from fate to a response: don't be thrown by reversal. The Purananuru poem goes further, withholding delight in life and resentment of it alike.
The epic turns the Naladiyar's maxim into a plot, which also raises a question the maxim avoids: Kannagi suffers through Kovalan's deed.

position: Birth is the same for all beings; distinction differs through the difference in what they do.
Those in high place who aren't high are not high; those in low place who aren't low are not low.
Manakkudavar: no difference among beings by birth.
A poem in Kalaignar's book says Valluvar rejected Manu's separate justice for each birth-based varna.
Every town is ours and everyone our kin.
We do not marvel at the great.
Still less do we scorn the small.
The learned are placed at the head, even if from the lowest place.
No one scorns the ferryman as lowest by old caste rule; take the learned as a guide likewise.
Excellence, gentleness and good conduct belong only to the high-born, even if others gain great wealth.
In his comment on the verse, Kalaignar says difference lies only in the skill shown in one's work.

note: The same book values the learned regardless of caste and reserves virtue for the high-born. An anthology by many hands may explain this, but the marks don't test that. Verse 136 also keeps the caste ranking while looking past it.

The Kural places distinction in what a person does; Naladiyar 142 places these virtues in lineage. Kural 951 says something close to Naladiyar 142, so the tension also runs inside the Kural: see the Kural-wide thread.

Both level social rank, on different grounds. Purananuru 192 refuses to rank at all, because all lives follow the same order. Kural 972 removes birth as a measure but keeps ranking by deeds. This is the subtle difference Agaram's test answer missed.

The verse's செய்தொழில் can mean deeds or occupation. Kalaignar's comment reads it as skill at one's work, while the poem in his book draws the anti-caste conclusion. On a reading tied to hereditary occupation, that conclusion would fit less easily, so the word carries the argument.

On the traditional reading, the bearer and rider of 37 show virtue's fruit in social position, which sits uneasily with 972's refusal to rank by birth. The two can be reconciled if position reflects past deeds, but that assumption is doing real work. Kalaignar's simile reading dissolves this tension.

position: Learn thoroughly, then stand by what was learned.
As a sand well yields with digging, knowledge flows with learning.
However many subtle books one reads, one's own understanding prevails.
Learning in one birth protects for seven.
The scholar's way is meeting with delight and leaving others wanting more.
No medicine like learning cures confusion.
Learning has no shore and the learner's days are few, so select as a bird takes milk from water.
Laughter among the learned sets a standard even heaven would have to beat.

note: Chapter 38 (fate) says innate understanding prevails over study. Chapter 40 (learning) says knowledge grows with study. Where a verse sits may matter: the same book frames knowledge differently under fate and under learning.
The Kural's image is depth: keep digging. The Naladiyar's is selection: time is short, so choose.
Both treat scholarly company as a pleasure, not only a means.

Both tie present conduct to future births: learning protects through them, and daily good blocks the road to them. The aims differ, protection in births versus ending them. Both rest on a rebirth reading that Kalaignar's commentary rejects: see 'One verse, different worldviews'.

position: A minister who knows the king's mind unspoken is an ornament to the world.
As crystal shows what is near, the face shows what is in the heart.
Eyes reveal enmity and friendship to those who can read them.
Her eyes hold two looks: one causes pain and the other cures it.
When I look she looks down; when I don't she looks and softly smiles.
Lovers themselves can glance as strangers do.
When eyes agree, words serve no purpose.

note: The Kural has two chapters titled குறிப்பறிதல்: 71 on statecraft and 110 on love. Both treat the eyes as a truer source than speech.

Chapter 71 trusts the face as a mirror of the heart. Chapter 110 shows lovers deliberately faking indifference, and the sign is read through the pretence. Signs can be honest or staged, so reading them takes skill.

position: Parimelazhagar: everything can become fate's route, so fate is the stronger.
Kalaignar: the natural state reasserts itself over artificial arrangements. Fate is not mentioned.
Parimelazhagar: good deeds are a stone blocking the way by which the soul rejoins a body.
Kalaignar: good deeds are a stone that paves the path of this life.
Parimelazhagar: virtue's fruit can be seen directly between the palanquin's bearer and rider.
Kalaignar: rider and bearer are similes for how the virtuous and the wicked carry life's joys and sorrows.
Kalaignar: learning protects through seven generations, not seven births of one person.
Kalaignar: natural intelligence prevails over study, in a verse from the chapter on fate.

note: The same word, ஊழ், is read as fate by one and as a natural condition by the other. That removes the cosmic agent from the verse.
The same stone blocks a road in one reading and paves it in the other, turning liberation from rebirth into a well-lived life.
Reading rider and bearer as similes removes the implication that social position shows past merit. It also bears on the Kural 37 and 972 tension in the birth thread.
Reading எழுமை as generations makes a metaphysical claim into a social one: educated families.
